summary: Defines IMAP4rev1, which lets a mail client access and manipulate electronic mail messages stored on a server. It was replaced by RFC 3501.

eli5.summary: Your email stays on the server, and your phone or computer looks at it from afar. IMAP is how they talk.

questions: what are the imap connection states
subtitle: Keep your email on a server and work with it from anywhere, as if the mailboxes were local.

tldr.problem: People want to read and organize mail that lives on a server, from different machines, without downloading and deleting it.
tldr.mechanism: A client sends tagged text commands over a reliable stream (TCP port 143). The server answers with untagged data lines and a final tagged OK, NO or BAD, working on mailboxes through four connection states.
tldr.outcome: IMAP4rev1 as defined here was obsoleted by RFC 3501.

today: RFC 2060 has been obsoleted by RFC 3501, so it is not the current IMAP4rev1 specification. It replaced RFC 1730 and its status here is Proposed Standard.

sections.title: What IMAP4rev1 Is
sections.content:
The Internet Message Access Protocol, Version 4rev1 (IMAP4rev1) lets a client access and manipulate electronic mail messages on a server. It treats remote message folders, called mailboxes, as functionally equivalent to local ones. Operations include creating, deleting and renaming mailboxes, checking for new messages, permanently removing messages, setting and clearing flags, searching, and selectively fetching parts of messages.

It does not send mail: posting is left to a mail transfer protocol such as SMTP. It supports a single server, and it is designed to be upwards compatible from IMAP2 and the unpublished IMAP2bis. Support for an offline client to resynchronize with the server is also a stated goal.

The RFC is written for implementors of clients and servers. It warns that the commands, responses and formal syntax are almost impossible to understand separately.
sections.eli5: IMAP lets you look after your mail while it stays on the mail server. It is for reading and sorting, and a different protocol is used for sending.

sections.title: Commands, Tags and Responses
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP, and a server listens on port 143. All traffic is lines ending in CRLF. Each client command starts with a tag, such as A0001, which the client makes different for every command.

The server's data lines start with an asterisk and are called untagged responses. A plus sign asks the client to continue, for example to send a literal. Each command ends with a tagged completion response that repeats the command's tag: OK for success, NO for failure, or BAD for a protocol error such as an unknown command or bad syntax. Tags let a client send several commands without waiting, but it must not do so when one command could change the result of another.

The server may send data the client never asked for, such as a new message count, and a client MUST be ready to accept any response at any time. Strings can be quoted strings or literals, which are an octet count in braces followed by the raw octets.
sections.eli5: Every question you ask gets a number label. The clerk answers with notes, and the last note repeats your label and says yes, no, or I did not understand.

sections.title: Message Numbers and Flags
sections.content:
A message can be named in two ways. The unique identifier (UID) is a 32-bit value that is assigned in strictly ascending order and, together with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY value, forms a 64-bit value that never refers to another message. If UIDs cannot be kept between sessions, the validity value MUST be larger than any used before.

The message sequence number is the message's position, from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox. It can change during a session: when a message is expunged, the sequence numbers of later messages go down by one.

Each message also has flags. The system flags are \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged, \Deleted, \Draft and \Recent. A message marked \Deleted is only removed when EXPUNGE is run. Servers can also define their own keywords. Other attributes are the internal date, the size, a parsed envelope and a parsed MIME body structure.
sections.eli5: Every letter has a permanent serial number and also a spot in the line that shifts when letters leave. Little stickers say whether it was read, answered or marked for the bin.

sections.title: The Four Connection States
sections.content:
A server is in one of four states, and most commands are valid in only some of them. In the non-authenticated state the client must supply credentials with LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE. In the authenticated state it can manage mailboxes and must SELECT or EXAMINE one before touching messages. In the selected state a mailbox is open, so commands such as FETCH, STORE, SEARCH, COPY and EXPUNGE work. The logout state ends the connection.

A connection starts non-authenticated, or authenticated if the greeting is PREAUTH, or goes straight to logout if the greeting is BYE. Only one mailbox can be selected at a time per connection. EXAMINE is like SELECT but read-only.

Three commands work in any state: CAPABILITY, NOOP and LOGOUT. A server inactivity timer, if there is one, must be at least 30 minutes.
sections.eli5: It is like a building: first the front door where you show who you are, then the hallway with all the mailrooms, then inside one mailroom. LOGOUT is the exit from anywhere.

sections.title: Mailbox Names
sections.content:
How mailbox names are read is up to the implementation, apart from INBOX, a case-insensitive name for the user's primary mailbox. Hierarchical names must be left to right and use a single separator character at every level. By convention, a first element starting with a hash sign names a namespace, for example #news for USENET newsgroups.

International names use a modified UTF-7. Printable US-ASCII characters stand for themselves, except &, which is written as an ampersand followed by a hyphen. Other characters go into modified BASE64 between an ampersand and a hyphen, using a comma instead of a slash. These changes avoid clashes with common hierarchy separators such as / and \.
sections.eli5: Folders have names, with INBOX as the special one for new mail. Names with unusual letters get written in a special code so they never get confused with the slashes that separate folders.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 traffic, including the mail itself, is sent in the clear unless privacy protection is negotiated in the AUTHENTICATE command. LOGIN sends the password in the clear, and the RFC says that can be avoided by using AUTHENTICATE instead.

Servers SHOULD NOT say why credentials were invalid, and a failing LOGIN SHOULD NOT reveal whether the user name or the password was the wrong one. AUTHENTICATE uses base64 challenges and answers and can optionally switch on integrity and privacy protection for the rest of the connection.
sections.eli5: Unless you use the safe way of logging in, your password and letters travel like postcards anyone could read. The clerk also should not tell a stranger whether the name or the password was wrong.
